title: Pluggable providers and filters
idea: An extensible notification service adds providers, retry behaviour and delivery rules as new classes wired by configuration, so the core send loop never changes.
points: Each delivery rule is a `NotificationFilter`; the service runs them as a chain.
`RetryingProvider` wraps any provider with retries, replacing the service's own retry loop.
A registry maps provider names to factories; config picks the failover order.
A builder assembles the filters once, then the service is immutable.

hero.title: Adding a vendor and a quiet-hours rule

left.title: Switch inside the service
items: New vendor means a new case in send
Quiet hours become another if in send
Retry logic copied into every vendor branch
Every change retests the whole service

right.title: Interfaces, decorator and registry
items: New vendor is one class plus one registry line
Quiet hours is one new filter class
Retries wrap any provider once, as a decorator
Failover order changes in config, not code

hero.verdict: The send loop is closed for edits and open for new classes.

code.title: Filter chain and builder
code.caption: Delivery rules as a chain. Quiet hours was added as a new class; the service did not change.

walk.text: The builder collects filters in order and builds the service.
Four requests: an OTP at night, a promo at night, and two daytime promos.
One method: return a reason to skip, or empty to let it pass.
Quiet hours span midnight. Critical messages such as OTPs always pass.
The first filter that rejects wins, and its reason is recorded.

code.title: Registry and decorator
code.caption: Vendors are registered by name and wrapped with retries. A config string picks the failover order. Booleans keep the demo short; the real decorator retries only RETRYABLE and returns REJECTED at once.

walk.text: Three vendor factories. vendor-c is the new one and fails a lot.
Wire two configs and send one SMS through each chain.
Unknown names fail at startup, not at the first send.
The decorator retries its inner provider and looks like any other provider.

pitfalls: Validate provider names when the service starts, not when the first message fails.
Do not put `if (vendor == ...)` in the service; register a new class instead.
Keep filter order explicit; a rate limit before opt-out wastes quota on muted users.

quiz.q: What is the last line ProviderConfig prints?
quiz.why: vendor-c is set to fail nine times, so its decorator gives up after two tries. The chain then fails over to vendor-a, which succeeds.

takeaway: New behaviour arrives as a new class plus one line of wiring.
